speaker_role: independent college essay coach and author (Ethan Sawyer, College Essay Guy)
commercial_incentive: Sells a book and paid resources/coaching; most materials linked are free, with a book mentioned.
key_insights: Three brainstorming exercises build a topic menu: objects that represent your essence, a values ranking from about 75 down to your top one, and 21 random facts about yourself.

Topic quality can be judged differently by type: montage essays by elasticity (how many sides of you it can show) and how uncommon it is; narrative essays by how compelling the challenge and insight are.
A common topic can still succeed if it is elastic; a challenge does not have to be extreme if the insight is strong.
Montage essays need not be about a challenge; he lists seven paths, e.g. things you love or know, a skill, essence objects, career, identities, home, or an uncommon activity.
Narrative essays should split roughly into challenge and effects, what you did about it, and what you learned; avoid forcing a challenge topic just because it seems expected.
Three ending techniques: a callback to the opening, a 'why us' setup that sequels into a school essay, and reserving explicit statement of values for the close.
Save common sports or instruments for supplemental essays rather than the personal statement.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker says the best essays often take more than five drafts.
Speaker says values list is about 75 items; the exercise runs 10 to 5 to 3 to 1.
Suggested times: 10 to 15 minutes for the essence-objects exercise.
notable_or_distinctive: Distinctive elasticity-versus-commonness framework and the montage/narrative structural taxonomy.
reliability_notes: Older video (about five years) from a coach, not an admissions officer; frameworks are his own and not evidence-tested.
